title: Overlap Rings
context: Grade 4, and two numbers are put side by side for the first time. An adult sees lists being compared. What is actually being carried is the difference from the topics before: comparing two lists that stop gives a shared list that stops, and comparing two lists that run on gives one that runs on, so common factors can be counted and common multiples cannot. The divide gate beside it is the shortcut the chapter offers once the lists have done their teaching, and it is the same single division that settles a factor question and a multiple question at once.

writeup.why: Find what two numbers have in common, and learn the single division that settles a multiple without writing any list at all.
writeup.look: Two rings of cord overlapping, filled with lists that stop or with tracks that do not, and a divide gate standing beside them.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Overlap Rings' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the cards lifted into the shared middle against the cards there are to test, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each card crosses and the second fixed at however many cards this phase laid out. In multiple mode the second number is replaced by an open dash rather than by a total, because that list has no length. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The two rings are drawn cord, each 470 across, centred at 420,430 and 700,430 so that they overlap through the middle of the working area, with the chosen number written on the outer edge of each. A third ring of the same size opens below and between them, centred at 560,600, when a third number is added, and the three overlaps are drawn rather than implied. In factor mode each ring fills with its number's factors as cards 84 by 84 laid in order between a wall at one and a wall at the number itself, so each list is visibly shut at both ends, and a card belonging to both lists travels into the overlap and takes the shared colour. In multiple mode the rings straighten into two parallel tracks, each 1086 by 8 at 64,352 and 64,472, running out through the right hand edge of the frame with no end mark and no last step drawn, and the overlap becomes a band 1086 by 112 at 64,368 that keeps catching new numbers as the tracks are run further and never closes. The divide gate stands at the right of the working area, 300 by 400 at 786,202: a bigger number and a smaller one are dropped into its mouth, the division is drawn on a ruled board as that many equal rows separated by walls, and whatever will not fit is set on the leftover shelf, 300 by 76 at 786,618, OUTSIDE the rows on the same surface at full strength and fully countable, never faded and never tucked under a row. Say both then writes the two statements that single division settled, the factor one and the multiple one, inside one frame under the shelf. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a common factor, a common multiple or a remainder is asked for, and on the second and fourth phases a word pad reading common, both, finite, infinite, factor and multiple, so that a shared list can be described as well as listed. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: a number that divides another exactly is deep blue, a number built by multiplying is green, anything standing in both lists at once is rose, whatever is left over and any trial that fails is vermilion, the number being broken up or the total in hand is amber, and a single digit being read or added is sky blue. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome, and every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a leftover is told by standing outside the rows before it is told by a band, and a list that stops is told by the wall at each end of it and a list that does not by the open edge of the frame. The two modes are never on the stage at once except where a phase asks for them to be, and when they are, the shut walls of the factor lists and the open edge of the tracks are drawn in the same frame at the same size. That single picture is the whole topic, and two written lists on a page cannot hold it.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last pair the child compared, both rings filled, the overlap still holding what they shared, and the gate's division beside it.

phases.win: the overlap holds exactly the common factors and each one divides both numbers
phases.does: fills each ring and moves whatever belongs to both into the overlap
phases.goal: a common factor is a number standing in both factor lists
phases.says: Fill both rings. Which numbers ended up standing in the middle?
phases.check: Find the common factors of 16 and 18, and say which of them you could have named before starting.
phases.feels: the middle holds only what stood in both lists, and one is always standing in it
phases.hands: Lay two loops of string on the floor so that they overlap, and write twenty-four on one and thirty-two on the other. Hand out number cards from one upward and let each child work out where their card belongs, in one loop, in the other, in the middle, or outside both. Before anybody names the middle, ask what every card lying in it has in common, and ask whether the middle could ever be left empty.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: does that card divide the first number exactly? Second rung, the phase's: does it divide the other one as well? Third rung: the rings are cut to two small numbers and the child fills both and lifts the shared cards across by hand. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: common sounds like putting the two lists together, and a middle full of cards looks like more of an answer than a middle holding four.
wrong.move: sweeps every factor of both numbers into the middle, so the overlap holds the two lists joined together.
wrong.screen: each card is picked up again and tested against both numbers as it crosses, the division for each drawn on the ruled board beside the rings with its leftover shelf showing. A card that divides only one of the two is set back into that ring rather than removed from the stage, and the middle is read out again once every card has been tested.

wrong.why: a number that turns up in every list anybody ever writes stops looking like a finding, and a child hunting for something interesting will step over it.
wrong.move: leaves one out of the middle because it goes into everything and so does not feel like an answer.
wrong.screen: one is dropped through the gate twice, twenty-four divided by one and thirty-two divided by one, each drawn on the board as a single row with the leftover shelf beside it empty. The card then travels into the middle and takes the shared colour like any other, and the middle is counted out with it in.

phases.screen: two empty rings with both factor lists waiting to be filled
phases.soWhat: A common factor divides both numbers, and one is a common factor of every pair of numbers.

phases.win: the band keeps catching numbers as the tracks run and no last meeting is drawn
phases.does: runs both tracks on and watches the shared band catch new numbers
phases.goal: two lists of multiples keep meeting, so the shared list has no end
phases.says: Keep both tracks running. Do they stop meeting? Could they?
phases.check: Write the first four common multiples of 6 and 8. Is there a greatest one? Say why.
phases.feels: one overlap kept filling and the other one shut
phases.hands: Write the multiples of two along one strip of paper and the multiples of three along another, and lay the two strips one above the other so that the numbers line up. Ring every number that appears on both. When the strips run out, stick more paper on the end of each and carry on, and ask whether the ringing is ever going to stop. Then write the factors of two and the factors of three underneath and ask the same question about those.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which numbers are standing in the band so far? Second rung, the phase's: what happens if both tracks take one more step? Third rung: the tracks are cut to two small step sizes and the child runs them until the band catches something twice. The word pad stays open.

wrong.why: that is where the two written lists stopped, and a list that has stopped looks exactly like a list that has finished.
wrong.move: writes six, twelve and eighteen and reports that those are all the common multiples there are.
wrong.screen: both tracks are run on past the end of the child's lists, one step at a time, and the band catches twenty-four, then thirty, then thirty-six, each meeting drawn as two flags sliding together. The three numbers the child wrote keep their own cards in the band, and the tracks and the band all leave the frame at the right with no end mark drawn on any of them.

wrong.why: both words carry common and both lists were built the same way, so a fact about one of them sounds like a fact about the pair of them.
wrong.move: carries the answer back the other way and says the common factors must be infinite too, since the common multiples are.
wrong.screen: the rings switch to factor mode on the very same two numbers. Two and three fill with their own factors, one and two in the first and one and three in the second, each penned between a wall at one and a wall at the number, and exactly one card travels into the overlap and the middle shuts. The multiple band is left running underneath it at the same time, so the shut middle and the open one are on the stage together.

phases.screen: the rings turned into two tracks leaving the frame with no end drawn
phases.soWhat: Common multiples never run out, because both of the lists they come from never run out.

phases.win: the gate returns an exact answer and the rings stay unused beside it
phases.does: runs the single division and reads the answer with nothing left over
phases.goal: one division settles whether a bigger number is a multiple of a smaller one
phases.says: Must you write both lists to find out? Try one division instead.
phases.check: Is 90 a multiple of 13? Settle it with one division and say what the division showed.
phases.feels: one division, and no list at all
phases.hands: Ask whether a hundred and eight is a multiple of nine, and start writing the multiples of nine on the board deliberately slowly, one line at a time. Partway through, stop and ask whether there is a faster way. Take the answer, do the single division beside the half written list, and leave both on the board together. Then hand out four pairs and let the class settle each one with one division.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which of the two numbers is the bigger one? Second rung, the phase's: what is left when you divide it by the other? Third rung: the gate is cut to two small numbers and the child runs the division and reads the shelf. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the lists are what the topic has been about for two sessions, and a question about multiples looks like a question that wants a list.
wrong.move: writes out the whole list of multiples of nine looking for a hundred and eight somewhere in it.
wrong.screen: the gate runs its single division on the ruled board beside the list the child is building, twelve rows of nine with nothing on the leftover shelf, and it has finished by the time the fourth line of the list is written. The child's list is left standing and is carried on to the twelfth line afterwards, so that both routes reach the same place and only one of them is short.

wrong.why: the question names the smaller number first and it is the number the child is thinking about, so it arrives at the front of the division.
wrong.move: divides the smaller number by the bigger one, because the smaller number is the one being asked about.
wrong.screen: the gate lays both ways round on the board one above the other. The smaller number divided by the bigger one puts no complete row on the board at all and sets the whole of it on the leftover shelf; the bigger divided by the smaller draws twelve equal rows with the shelf empty. Both boards stay drawn and nothing is marked.

phases.screen: the divide gate loaded with a bigger and a smaller number and the rings dimmed
phases.soWhat: To find out whether a bigger number is a multiple of a smaller one, divide the bigger by the smaller.
phases.concept: One division instead of two lists

phases.win: the leftover stands outside the rows and both statements are written under it
phases.does: counts what is left over and writes both statements the division settled
phases.goal: anything left over settles the factor question and the multiple question at once
phases.says: Something is left over. Say the two things that tells you.
phases.check: Divide 38 by 6, then write the two things that one division has settled.
phases.feels: the leftover answered two questions at once
phases.hands: Put fifty-five counters on the table and share them into seven equal rows. Push whatever will not fit into the middle where everybody can see it and count it out loud. Then ask two questions about that one pile: is fifty-five a multiple of seven, and is seven a factor of fifty-five. Write both answers down and ask how many divisions it took to get them.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many are standing on the shelf? Second rung, the phase's: what does anything on the shelf say about these two numbers? Third rung: the gate is cut to two small numbers that will not come out and the child reads the shelf and writes both lines. The word pad stays open.

wrong.why: six out of fifty-five is a small enough miss to feel like an accident of the numbers rather than an answer, and seven sevens sitting there in neat rows look like a success.
wrong.move: sees a small leftover and calls seven nearly a factor of fifty-five.
wrong.screen: the six are drawn on the shelf outside the rows at full strength and counted one at a time. The seven rows are counted beside them and read as forty-nine, against a tray of fifty-five. The gate then asks what would have to be true of the tray for seven to be a factor of it, and the child's verdict stays in the slot throughout.

wrong.why: the question that was asked out loud was about multiples, and an answer to the question asked feels finished.
wrong.move: writes the multiple statement and leaves the factor one unsaid, as though the division had settled one question and not two.
wrong.screen: say both opens under the shelf and writes the two statements into one frame, with the same division lit behind each of them in turn, and with the leftover still standing outside the rows above them. The statement the child did write stays exactly where it was written and the second is drawn beside it rather than over it.

phases.screen: the gate holding a division that does not come out, with the leftover showing
phases.soWhat: A remainder says the bigger number is not a multiple of the smaller, and that the smaller is not a factor of the bigger.

writeup.delight: The second phase, once both tracks are running. A number that is caught by the band is not simply coloured in: the flag on the upper track and the flag on the lower track are drawn sliding towards each other until they meet in the band, where they become one card in the shared colour, and the two steps that brought them there stay drawn behind it. Run the tracks further and it happens again, and again, with the gap between the meetings always the same length. A child who holds keep going down long enough sees the whole stage scroll through meeting after meeting, and the shared band leaves the frame as open at its right hand end as the two tracks do.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase two rings of cord lie overlapping with a number written on each and both of them empty, and the factor cards wait in a row beneath. On the second the rings have already straightened into two parallel tracks that leave the frame at the right with no end mark, each carrying a few flags, and the shared band lies along them holding nothing yet. On the third the rings are dimmed right back and the divide gate stands lit beside them with a bigger number and a smaller one already loaded. On the fourth the gate holds a division that will not come out, with the board ruled and the leftover shelf beside it empty. The running count at the top left holds the cards lifted into the shared middle against the cards there are to test, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the empty overlap, or the shared band, or the gate's mouth, or the leftover shelf, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what these two numbers are going to have in common. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any two or three numbers in the rings, either mode, with the divide gate open beside them. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on finding what two or three numbers share, listing common multiples, settling a multiple with one division, and reading what a remainder rules out.
voiceLines: Two rings, overlapping in the middle. Something is going to end up in there.
Fill both rings. Which numbers ended up standing in the middle?
Keep both tracks running. Do they stop meeting? Could they?
Must you write both lists to find out? Try one division instead.
Something is left over. Say the two things that tells you.
Two new numbers, one to a ring. What are they going to share?
Free play. Any numbers in the rings, either mode, the gate open beside them.
Fill both lists again and lift across only what is standing in each of them.
One overlap you could count, and one that kept on catching new numbers.

observations.why: One divides every number there is, so it is in both lists whatever the two numbers are.
observations.soWhat: One is a common factor of every pair of numbers, and the overlap is never empty.
observations.observe: Something was standing in the overlap before either list had been fully read.

observations.why: Both factor lists shut at their own numbers, while both lists of multiples run on for ever and so keep meeting.
observations.soWhat: Common factors can be counted and common multiples cannot, and no greatest common multiple exists.
observations.observe: The factor overlap filled and then stopped, and the multiple band never stopped.

observations.why: Dividing the bigger number by the smaller one tests the only thing the lists were going to be searched for.
observations.soWhat: One division settles whether a bigger number is a multiple of a smaller one.
observations.observe: The gate answered without either ring being filled at all.

observations.why: The division that failed to come out is the same division that answers both questions.
observations.soWhat: A remainder says it is not a multiple and that the smaller number is not a factor, at one stroke.
observations.observe: What was left over on the shelf was written into two statements, not one.

description: Fill two rings and look at what falls in both, then settle a multiple with one division instead of two whole lists.

serves.exercise: finding the common factors of the four given sets of numbers
writing the first six multiples of each of the two given numbers and finding their common multiples
finding the first four common multiples of the two given numbers

source_tool.description: Two large rings of cord overlap in the middle of the stage, one for each of two chosen numbers. In factor mode each ring fills with that number's factors, penned between walls at both ends so each list is plainly finished, and whatever belongs to both drifts into the overlap and changes to the shared colour. One always lands in the overlap, whatever the two numbers are, and the tool lets that be noticed rather than telling it. A third ring can be opened for a third number, because the printed work asks for that once without warning. In multiple mode the rings become two tracks running off the right hand edge with no end drawn, and the overlap becomes a band along them that keeps catching new numbers as the tracks run, so this overlap is seen never to close. A divide gate stands beside the rings. A bigger number and a smaller one are dropped into it, one division runs, and the answer comes out with any remainder drawn OUTSIDE the rows at full strength. The gate then writes both of the things that one division settled: whether the bigger is a multiple of the smaller, and whether the smaller is a factor of the bigger.
source_tool.art_direction: Two overlapping rings and a divide gate / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: trays of countable things, ruled rows on a board, a ladder of rungs with one trial to a rung, a pen with a wall at each end, a track of equal steps, cards that turn over, and two rings of cord that overlap.

Equal groups are drawn genuinely equal and genuinely countable. Where a row is labelled with a number, exactly that many things are in it, and the rows are kept apart by a drawn wall or a plain gap and never by colour alone.

Whatever is left over is drawn OUTSIDE the rows, on the same surface, at full strength and fully countable. It is never faded, never crossed out, never tucked under a row and never left to be guessed from a gap. The leftover is the reason a trial failed, so it is the last thing any stage may hide.

A list of factors is drawn penned in between one and the number itself, with both ends of the run plainly stopped by a wall or a final post, so the list can be seen to end. A list of multiples is drawn running from the number away to the right, and the track carrying it leaves the frame with no end mark and no last step drawn, so the list can be seen not to end. The two never run the same way on one stage.

A run of trials is drawn unbroken. Every whole number from one up to the last one tried keeps its own rung or row, in order, with none left out, and a trial that fails is drawn and marked as a failure rather than dropped.
Where the digits of a number are added, every digit sits in its own cell, zeros included, and a cell holding a zero is drawn and counted in rather than left out of the line.
Nothing the child is asked to count one at a time comes to more than twenty things in one group. A larger quantity is a ruled array of identical tiles or a written numeral, never a loose heap.
A list is told apart by the wall or the open edge at its end first and by its band second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a number, a counter or a card the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. A number that divides another exactly is deep blue, a number that is built by multiplying is green, and anything standing in both lists at once is rose, and those three hold in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Whatever is left over, and any trial that fails, is vermilion; the number being broken up or the total in hand is amber; and a single digit being read or added is sky blue. All of that holds in greyscale, because a failed trial is told apart by the leftover drawn outside its row before it is told apart by colour, and a factor list is told apart from a list of multiples by the wall at each end of it before either is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Fill both lists again and lift across only what is standing in each of them.
voice.onNext: Two new numbers, one to a ring. What are they going to share?
voice.opening: Two rings, overlapping in the middle. Something is going to end up in there.
voice.onFinish: One overlap you could count, and one that kept on catching new numbers.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any numbers in the rings, either mode, the gate open beside them.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: One division instead of two lists

placement.where: After two lists have been written out by hand on paper and the shared numbers ringed with a pencil. The tool is what keeps one overlap closing and the other refusing to, side by side on one stage, which two written lists cannot show at once.

answer_key.rule: A common factor of two numbers divides both of them exactly, and it is found by writing both factor lists and taking what appears in each. One is a common factor of every pair of numbers, because one is a factor of everything. A common multiple appears in both lists of multiples, and because both of those lists run on for ever they keep meeting for ever, so there are infinitely many common multiples and no greatest one. To find out whether a bigger number is a multiple of a smaller one you do not need either list: divide the bigger by the smaller and look at what is left. Nothing over means it is a multiple, and the same division says the smaller number is a factor of the bigger.
answer_key.wrong: The two lists are laid out again side by side with the shared numbers lifting into the overlap one at a time, and the gate redoes its division as rows with the remainder set outside them. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The numbers standing in both lists are 1, 2, 7 and 14, and each of them divides 42 and 70 exactly.
items.question: Write the factors of 42 and the factors of 70, and say which numbers turn up in both.
items.checkpoint: A common factor divides both numbers, and it is found by comparing the two lists.
items.misconception: Listing every factor of both numbers together, instead of keeping only the ones in both.

steps: Both lists of multiples run on for ever, so they go on meeting for ever.
After 36 the next meeting is 48, then 60, then 72, and so on with no end.
Common multiples never run out, which is the opposite of common factors.
items.answer: No. There are infinitely many, and 48, 60 and 72 come next
items.question: The multiples of 4 and the multiples of 6 meet at 12, 24 and 36. Is that all of them?
items.checkpoint: Common multiples go on for ever, because both lists they come from do.
items.misconception: Thinking the meetings stop where the written lists stop, rather than where the lists stop being written.

steps: To test a bigger number against a smaller one, divide the bigger by the smaller.
112 divided by 8 comes out exactly at 14, with nothing left over.
So 112 is a multiple of 8, and the same division says 8 is a factor of 112.
items.answer: Yes, because 112 divided by 8 is 14 with nothing over
items.question: Is 112 a multiple of 8? Find out without writing either list.
items.checkpoint: One division settles whether a bigger number is a multiple of a smaller one.
items.misconception: Writing out the whole list of multiples of 8 to look for 112 in it.

steps: 74 divided by 9 is 8 with 2 left over, and those 2 stay outside the rows.
Anything left over means 74 is not a multiple of 9.
The very same division says 9 does not divide 74 exactly, so 9 is not a factor of it.
items.answer: That 74 is a multiple of 9, and that 9 is a factor of 74
items.question: Divide 74 by 9. What does the answer rule out?
items.checkpoint: A remainder settles the factor question and the multiple question at the same time.
items.misconception: Deciding that 9 is nearly a factor because the leftover is small.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Find the common factors of 20 and 34.
Why is 1 a common factor of every pair of numbers you could pick?
items.final_answer: Because 1 is a factor of every number, so it has to appear in both lists

items.question: Is 45 a multiple of 5?
items.final_answer: Yes, because 45 divided by 5 is 9 with nothing over

items.question: Write the first four common multiples of 4 and 10.
Is 126 a multiple of 7?
items.final_answer: Yes, because 126 divided by 7 is 18 with nothing over

items.question: Find the common factors of 30, 45 and 75.
Divide 135 by 8 and say what that rules out.
items.final_answer: 135 divided by 8 is 16 with 7 left over, so 135 is not a multiple of 8 and 8 is not a factor of 135

items.question: In the board game you throw a 4 and want to move onto 57. Divide to find out whether you may.
items.final_answer: No. 57 divided by 4 is 14 with 1 left over, so 57 is not a multiple of 4

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: gives each chosen number a ring of its own, overlapping in the middle
opens a ring for a third number when the work asks for one
fills each ring with a factor list penned between walls at both ends
turns the rings into tracks running off the edge with no end drawn
moves anything belonging to both lists into the shared middle
runs one division on a bigger and a smaller number and shows the remainder
writes the factor statement and the multiple statement that one division settled

teaching_notes: Lay two string rings on the floor first, hand out number cards, and let the children put themselves in the right ring or in the overlap. Ask what the overlap holds before naming it, and ask whether the overlap could ever be empty; the answer, that one is always in it, is worth arriving at rather than being told. Then switch to multiples and ask the same question again, and let the class notice that this time the overlap keeps filling and there is no greatest number in it. Holding those two answers together is the whole topic. The divide gate comes last and comes as a shortcut, never as the first method, because a child who divides before ever comparing two lists has the answer and not the idea. When a division leaves something over, stop and get both statements said aloud, because they are one fact and children treat them as two. The closing board game is this tool as a race: a throw names a divisor, and one division decides whether the cell you want is legal.
generation_prompt: Build a shared list tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. Two large rings of drawn cord overlap in the middle, each labelled with one chosen number, with an optional third ring that opens when a third number is added. In factor mode each ring fills with that number's factors as cards laid in order between a wall at one and a wall at the number itself, so each list is visibly closed at both ends, and any card belonging to both lists animates into the overlap and takes the shared colour. In multiple mode the rings straighten into two parallel tracks that leave the frame at the right hand edge with no end mark and no last step drawn, and the overlap becomes a band along them that keeps catching new numbers as the tracks are run further, never closing. A divide gate stands beside the rings: a bigger and a smaller number are dropped in, the division is drawn as equal rows on a ruled board, and any remainder is set outside the rows at full strength and fully countable, never faded. A say both control then writes the two statements that single division settled, one about factors and one about multiples, in the same frame. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Put a number in each ring and fill both lists. Move anything in both into the middle. Switch to multiples and run the tracks on. Then use the gate: divide the bigger number by the smaller one and look at what is left over.
